content: Hypoxaemia during labour can lead to changes in the fetal electrocardiogram (ECG) waveform, particularly in the relationship between the PR and RR intervals, as well as in the elevation or depression of the ST segment. To address this, technical systems have been developed to monitor fetal ECG during labour as a supplement to continuous electronic fetal heart rate monitoring. The goal of these systems is to improve fetal outcomes while reducing unnecessary obstetric interventions. A systematic review was conducted to compare the effects of fetal ECG waveform analysis during labour with other methods of fetal monitoring. The review included seven randomised trials involving a total of 27,403 women. Six of these trials focused on ST waveform analysis (26,446 women), while one trial examined PR interval analysis (957 women). The trials were generally assessed as having a low risk of bias, and the quality of evidence for ST waveform analysis was graded as moderate to high. When compared to continuous electronic fetal heart rate monitoring alone, the addition of ST waveform analysis did not result in significant differences in key outcomes. Specifically, there was no notable reduction in the rate of caesarean births (risk ratio [RR] 1.02, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.96 to 1.08; six trials, 26,446 women; high-quality evidence). Similarly, there was no clear reduction in the number of babies born with severe metabolic acidosis (cord arterial pH < 7.05 and base deficit > 12 mmol/L) (average RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.20; six trials, 25,682 babies; moderate-quality evidence) or neonatal encephalopathy (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.22; six trials, 26,410 babies; high-quality evidence). However, the use of ST waveform analysis was associated with fewer fetal scalp samples being taken during labour (average RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.91; four trials, 9,671 babies; high-quality evidence). It is important to note that these findings were heterogeneous, and data from the largest trial (conducted in the USA) were not included. Additionally, there were slightly fewer operative vaginal births (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.86 to 0.99; six trials, 26,446 women). There was no significant difference in the number of babies with low Apgar scores at five minutes, those requiring neonatal intubation, or those needing admission to a special care unit (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.04; six trials, 26,410 babies; high-quality evidence). In contrast, there was little evidence to suggest that PR interval analysis provided any clinical benefit. The findings did not demonstrate improvements in any outcomes, and further research, potentially involving larger trials, may be needed to explore its potential benefits. The authors concluded that while ST waveform analysis may offer modest benefits, such as fewer fetal scalp samplings and fewer instrumental vaginal births, these advantages must be weighed against the need for an internal scalp electrode, which requires membrane rupture. There was limited evidence to suggest that ST waveform analysis significantly impacted primary outcomes. Additionally, there was no strong evidence to support the use of PR interval analysis. The review highlighted a lack of data on the use of fetal ECG waveform monitoring in preterm fetuses during labour and emphasized the need for information on the long-term developmental outcomes of the babies included in these trials.
